UMD wasn't too bad, but I don't think Nintendo has the resources to develop their own storage medium. Sony has a huge advantage because they're way more than a gaming company and Playstation is just a piece of the pie for them (though it's grown quite large lately). Wii U uses "not" Blu Ray, it's basically entirely Blu Ray but with no licensing so it can't play Blu Ray Discs.

It's a lot easier to solder some memory chips to a PCB and call it done, than it is to have an optical drive with a motor to rotate the disc, and a motor to move the lens. I really am hoping we go back to carts. Optical storage rots and only has a shelf life of 5 to 20 years (depending on disc quality). My NES still works, so do all the games from when I was a little kid (minus dead batteries for things like save games). But my CDs from when I was in high school? A lot of them don't work that well anymore, if at all (read errors and stuff). The CDRs actually have visible rot to them.

Not to mention there's hardly any seek time, meaning you can stream stuff from the storage medium instead of having to install it. If NX really is a handheld and a console, think of the games you have to install on modern consoles before playing them. NX, if it really is two devices, would require you to install the game twice, once on the handheld, one on the console. Decent quality flash memory could easily bypass install requirements and stuff like that.

UMD's highest capacity was 1.8GB with dual layer. The closest existing optical technology I can find is a mini BD, which is 8cm large and holds 16.5GB. There's some other interesting emerging technology (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Optical_disc#Fourth-generation), but none of it seems to be small. Considering 3DS carts hold 8GB max and are probably using out dated fabrication process for the memory (you know, like nm for your CPUs and GPUs), and new technology is coming out soon. Generally, one part of making a chip like that gets more expensive, but you can make more per run, so it ends up worth it. Which is why if Nintendo holds off for new memory technology they could have a cost per GB advantage even over the 3DS carts they sell for $40.

But as for the nail in optical's coffin, I actually found Macronix ROM specs for their memory. http://www.macronix.com/CachePages/en-us-Product-ROM-default.aspx#128Mb (100ns is 0.0001ms) 7200rpm hard drive is around 4.7ms (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_disk_drive_performance_characteristics This Blu Ray drive is around 79ms and can take over a third of a second to find data on the disc (http://www.pcstats.com/articleview.cfm?articleid=2347&page=5)

Nintendo going with carts would make installing anything on a console completely futile and no longer needed. It would actually be a really great thing, the load times would be extremely short, even compared to a HD in Xbone or PS4. And finally, if you want to do an experiment to see just how much seek time and latency affect a computer (and the consoles are just specialized computers), try installing Linux on an SSD, and then try using a live CD or live DVD where you run the entire OS off of optical storage.
